title: John Brown at Charles Town
subtitle: The Harpers Ferry raid, the Virginia trials and the Senate inquiry, 1859–1860
intro: On the night of Sunday 16 October 1859 John Brown led twenty-one men into Harpers Ferry, Virginia, and seized the federal armory, meaning to arm enslaved people and start a war on slavery from the mountains. Thirty-six hours later Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee broke into the engine house where he had made his stand. Ten raiders were dead, two of them his sons, along with four men of the town and district, among them the free Black baggage master Heyward Shepherd, and one Marine. Brown, wounded, was questioned on the floor of the paymaster's office by a senator, a congressman and a crowd of reporters.

What followed was a trial that both sides treated as a stage. Virginia tried Brown in its own county court at Charles Town, not in a federal court, and moved fast: indictment on 26 October, verdict on 31 October, sentence on 2 November, hanging on 2 December. His men followed him to the gallows on 16 December and 16 March. In the meantime Brown wrote letter after letter from his cell, and newspapers North and South printed them, along with his interview and his speech before sentence.

The record here is mixed and the form tags say so. The court's formal papers survive, but the proceedings are known mainly from reporters' shorthand and from pamphlets put together by one side or the other. Brown's own words come through those reporters and through his manuscript letters. Around them stand an official US Army report, a governor's papers, letters between strangers that were printed as a pamphlet, public lectures, a soldier's letter, a secessionist's diary, two condemned men's letters, a raider's memoir written later, and a Senate report with two opposed conclusions.

The eyes divide sharply. Lee called the plan the work of a fanatic or madman; Governor Wise called its leader brave and truthful and then refused him mercy; Senator Mason and his wife saw Northern money and the threat of a slave rising. Thoreau in Concord and Lydia Maria Child in Wayland, saw a man of principle; Frederick Douglass, named in the captured papers, wrote from Canada to deny that he had promised to come. Osborne Anderson, who escaped, and John Copeland, who did not, are the two Black raiders whose words survive. Victor Hugo's plea from Guernsey was written on the day of the hanging.

This chapter gives no verdict on the raid or the trial. It sets out what each side wrote, and it records the deaths, of raiders, townspeople and a Marine, without dwelling on them. The epilogue is the Senate's inquiry under Mason, which heard the same testimony and returned two reports: one blaming Northern backers, one saying the free states had no part in it.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and need no conversion. The town was then usually spelled Charlestown, Virginia; it is Charles Town, West Virginia, today, and the record uses both spellings. Several sources disagree on the day of the verdict: the court dates followed by the West Virginia Archives put it on Monday 31 October, with sentence on 2 November; at least one popular chronology conflates the two.

eyes.name: John Brown
eyes.role: Abolitionist, aged 59; leader of the Harpers Ferry raid; wounded and captured 18 October, tried and hanged at Charles Town
eyes.where: Kennedy farm, Maryland; the Harpers Ferry armory; Jefferson County jail, Charles Town
eyes.form: dated letters from jail; reported interview; speech in court as reported; last written note
eyes.authenticity: The 18 October interview survives only as reporters' versions (the New York Herald's is the fullest); the speech at sentencing is known from newspaper shorthand reports, which differ in small wording. His jail letters survive in manuscript in several collections (the Boyd B. Stutler Collection, West Virginia Archives, among them) and were printed by F. B. Sanborn (1885; 1910). The last note, handed to a guard on 2 December, survives in manuscript.
eyes.bio: Brown had fought in Kansas in 1856 and planned for years to strike at slavery in Virginia. After the raid failed he turned the courtroom and the jail into a pulpit, writing scores of letters to family and sympathisers. His words were printed North and South while he was still alive.

sources.title: Interview in the Charlestown prison (Sanborn transcription, marxists.org)
Letter to his family, 31 Oct 1859, with 2 Nov postscript (West Virginia Archives)
Speech at sentencing (Digital History)

eyes.name: Circuit Court of Jefferson County, Virginia (Judge Richard Parker)
eyes.role: State court trying the raiders; Judge Richard Parker; prosecutors Charles Harding and Andrew Hunter; defence Lawson Botts, Thomas C. Green, then George H. Hoyt, Samuel Chilton and Hiram Griswold
eyes.form: court record (indictments, orders, sentences) with reporters' accounts of proceedings
eyes.authenticity: The formal papers (indictments, orders, sentences) are held by the Jefferson County Circuit Clerk. The day-by-day proceedings, testimony and speeches are known mainly from reporters' shorthand printed in the New York Herald and Tribune and gathered in pamphlets such as The Life, Trial and Execution of Captain John Brown (New York, 1859). These are partisan in selection, not an official transcript.
eyes.bio: The court moved fast: arraignment nine days after the capture, a verdict a fortnight later. The defence argued that Brown, a non-Virginian, owed the state no allegiance and so could not commit treason against it; for Copeland and Green it argued that under Dred Scott they were not citizens at all.

sources.title: West Virginia Archives, John Brown exhibit, ch. 11: the trials
Famous Trials: The Trial of John Brown
Battlefields: Witnesses and testimony at the trial

eyes.name: Robert E. Lee
eyes.role: Brevet colonel, US Army, aged 52; on leave at Arlington, sent to command the Marines and militia at Harpers Ferry
eyes.vantage_label: the commander who stormed the engine house
eyes.form: official report and written summons (US government record)
eyes.authenticity: The written summons of 18 October and the report of 19 October to the Adjutant General are in the National Archives (RG 94) and were printed in the Senate committee's 1860 report. US-government records; quotable.
eyes.bio: Lee's report is the government's first account: casualties listed by name, the plan judged hopeless. Its dry tone is the opposite of the speeches that followed. Lee later testified before the Senate committee.

sources.title: Col. R. E. Lee's report, 19 Oct 1859 (Encyclopedia Virginia)
Lee's demand for surrender, 18 Oct 1859 (DocsTeach, National Archives)

eyes.name: Henry A. Wise
eyes.role: Governor of Virginia, aged 53; hurried to Harpers Ferry, questioned Brown, and controlled clemency
eyes.where: Richmond; Harpers Ferry and Charles Town
eyes.vantage_label: the governor who held the pardon
eyes.authenticity: Executive papers at the Library of Virginia; his Richmond speech of 21 October as printed in the press (National Era, 3 Nov 1859); his letter to Lydia Maria Child printed in the 1860 pamphlet.
eyes.bio: Wise both praised Brown's nerve and insisted on his execution. His published reply to Lydia Maria Child made him one of the voices of the Southern case in the Northern press.

sources.title: Library of Virginia: Gov. Wise documents
Extract of Wise's speech, 21 Oct 1859 (Civil War Notebook)

eyes.name: James Murray Mason
eyes.role: US senator from Virginia, aged 61; questioned Brown on 18 October; chaired the Senate's select committee on the raid
eyes.authenticity: His questions survive in reporters' versions of the 18 October interview. The committee's report (Senate Rep. Com. No. 278, 36th Cong., 1st sess., 15 June 1860), with testimony and a minority view, is a printed US-government record.
eyes.bio: Mason was among the first to question the wounded Brown, pressing him on who had sent and funded him. He then led the Senate inquiry into Northern backers, which jailed a reluctant witness and ended in split reports.

sources.title: Mason committee report, 15 June 1860 (West Virginia Archives)
Senate Historical Office: 'Senate Prisoner Goes Free'

eyes.name: Osborne Perry Anderson
eyes.role: Free Black printer from Pennsylvania living at Chatham, Canada West, aged 29; one of the raiders, posted at the arsenal
eyes.where: Harpers Ferry arsenal; escape through Pennsylvania to Canada
eyes.authenticity: A Voice from Harper's Ferry (Boston, 'printed for the author', 1861), written with editorial help; the preface is signed O. P. A. It is an insider's account written after the event and partisan to Brown; it gives few exact dates for the escape.
eyes.bio: Anderson was the only Black raider to survive and escape, and his book is the only account by a raider who was neither hanged nor writing under sentence. He insists that enslaved men of the district joined the raid, a point disputed by Southern accounts.

sources.title: A Voice from Harper's Ferry (Project Gutenberg)
West Virginia Archives edition

eyes.name: John Anthony Copeland Jr.
eyes.role: Free Black carpenter and Oberlin student from North Carolina and Ohio, about 25; captured at Hall's rifle works; hanged 16 December
eyes.where: Harpers Ferry rifle works; Charles Town jail
eyes.authenticity: His letters of 10 and 16 December 1859 were printed in 1859–60 (including as a broadside, Howard University) and are transcribed by Oberlin College from degraded copies; some words are unreadable.
eyes.bio: Copeland had been part of the 1858 Oberlin–Wellington rescue of a fugitive. In jail he wrote to his family placing the raid in a line from the Revolution, and asking them not to grieve.

sources.title: The Letters of John A. Copeland (Oberlin College)
Letters of John A. Copeland, broadside 1859 (Howard University)

eyes.name: Henry David Thoreau
eyes.role: Writer and surveyor, aged 42; had met Brown in Concord in 1857 and 1859
eyes.vantage_label: Northern defender, far from the court
eyes.authenticity: 'A Plea for Captain John Brown' was read at Concord on 30 October 1859 and repeated in Boston and Worcester; printed in Echoes of Harper's Ferry (1860). His journal also records the weeks of the trial.
eyes.bio: Thoreau spoke when almost every Northern paper was calling Brown insane. He defended Brown's character, not his acquittal, and his lecture set the tone for the sympathetic Northern response.

sources.title: Famous Trials: Thoreau, A Plea for Captain John Brown

eyes.name: Lydia Maria Child
eyes.role: Author and abolitionist, aged 57; asked Governor Wise for leave to nurse Brown in jail
eyes.vantage_label: the would-be nurse who argued by letter
eyes.authenticity: Correspondence between Lydia Maria Child and Gov. Wise and Mrs. Mason, of Virginia (Boston: American Anti-Slavery Society, 1860). Letters first appeared in the New York Tribune and other papers; the pamphlet was edited by her side.
eyes.bio: Child never reached Charles Town. Her exchange with Wise and with Senator Mason's wife became one of the most widely read pamphlets of 1860, a debate on slavery conducted in letters between three people who never met.

sources.title: The 1860 pamphlet (West Virginia Archives)
Excerpt, Mason and Child (American Yawp Reader)

eyes.name: Margaretta Mason (Mrs. M. J. C. Mason)
eyes.role: Wife of Senator James M. Mason, about 58; writing from her home in King George County
eyes.authenticity: Her letter of 11 November 1859 was printed in the newspapers and in the 1860 pamphlet (pp. 16–19). Signed 'M. J. C. Mason'.
eyes.bio: Mrs. Mason wrote unasked to rebuke Child, defending Virginia slaveholders as Christian carers and describing what she feared a slave rising would have meant. Her letter is the fullest woman's voice on the Southern side in this record.

sources.title: Mrs. M. J. C. Mason to Lydia Maria Child (Civil War Notebook)

eyes.name: Frederick Douglass
eyes.role: Abolitionist editor in Rochester, aged about 41; had met Brown at Chambersburg in August 1859 and declined to join
eyes.where: Rochester, then Canada West, then England
eyes.vantage_label: named in the papers, out of reach
eyes.authenticity: His letter dated Canada West, 31 October 1859, appeared in the Rochester Democrat and was widely reprinted (e.g. New Orleans Picayune, 9 Nov 1859). His later account in Life and Times (1881) is a memoir written later.
eyes.bio: Papers found at the Kennedy farm named Douglass, and Virginia wanted him. From Canada he denied that he had ever promised to join the raid while refusing to disown Brown.

sources.title: 'Frederick Douglass's Letter', New Orleans Picayune, 9 Nov 1859 (House Divided)

eyes.name: Thomas J. Jackson
eyes.role: Major and professor at the Virginia Military Institute, aged 35; with the VMI cadet detachment at the execution
eyes.authenticity: Letter to his wife Mary Anna, 2 December [1859] (year bracketed by editors); original in the Dabney–Jackson collection, Library of Virginia; printed in Mary Anna Jackson's Life and Letters (1892).
eyes.bio: Later famous as 'Stonewall', Jackson was then a teacher of natural philosophy. His letter is a plain eyewitness description by a deeply religious man who prayed for Brown as he watched.

sources.title: VMI Archives: John Brown execution eyewitness

eyes.name: Edmund Ruffin
eyes.where: Charles Town; then Richmond and Washington
eyes.authenticity: Manuscript diary at the Library of Congress; published as The Diary of Edmund Ruffin, ed. W. K. Scarborough (LSU Press, 1972–89). Modern edition: digests only, no quotation.
eyes.bio: Ruffin saw the raid as proof that the South must leave the Union. He went to Charles Town, stood with the VMI cadets at the hanging, and turned Brown's pikes into propaganda.

sources.title: 'Martyrs to their cause': Brown, Ruffin and Harpers Ferry (Civil War Monitor)

eyes.name: Victor Hugo
eyes.role: French poet and novelist, aged 57; in political exile
eyes.where: Hauteville House, St Peter Port, Guernsey
eyes.authenticity: Open letter dated 2 December 1859, sent to the London News and widely reprinted in translation; his drawing of the hanged Brown was engraved in 1860. French original: digests only.
eyes.bio: Hugo wrote to the American republic asking it to spare Brown, not knowing that the execution had been fixed for the very day he wrote. The letter made Brown a European cause.

sources.title: Tufts: Victor Hugo and John Brown
English text on Wikisource

entries.headline: Twenty-one men march on the armory
entries.digest: Brown led a party of about twenty-one men, five of them Black, from the Maryland farm across the Potomac bridge. They seized the federal armory, arsenal and Hall's rifle works and sent parties to take hostages from nearby farms, among them Colonel Lewis W. Washington. A free Black baggage master, Heyward Shepherd, was shot on the bridge that night.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11; Famous Trials chronology (via mail.famous-trials.com); Lee's report, 19 Oct 1859.

entries.headline: Posted at the arsenal with Hazlett
entries.digest: Anderson was ordered to hold the arsenal with Albert Hazlett. He later wrote that enslaved men from the neighbourhood came in once word was sent round, and that he was told to hand out pikes to them. Southern accounts denied that local slaves joined willingly; the two versions have never been reconciled.
entries.source_note: Anderson, A Voice from Harper's Ferry (1861), Project Gutenberg 73843; memoir written later, no hour given.

entries.headline: The governor leaves his office in a hurry
entries.digest: As news of the raid arrived, Wise wrote a short order authorising Colonel George W. Munford to sign his name and act for him while a sudden emergency called him away. He then set out for Harpers Ferry.
entries.source_note: Wise to Munford, 17 Oct 1859, Library of Virginia executive papers (LVA PDF).

entries.headline: Trapped at the rifle works
entries.digest: Copeland was with John Kagi and Lewis Leary at the rifle works when militia attacked across the Shenandoah. Kagi and Leary were killed and Copeland was taken alive. Anderson later wrote that Copeland met his fate like a man.
entries.source_note: Anderson, A Voice from Harper's Ferry (1861); Lee's report lists Copeland among prisoners. Hour of capture not fixed.

entries.headline: Lee arrives and waits for daylight
entries.digest: Lee reached the town that night with a detachment of Marines. He decided not to attack in the dark for fear of killing the hostages held in the armory's engine house, and planned an assault at first light.
entries.source_note: Lee's report, 19 Oct 1859 (Encyclopedia Virginia).

entries.headline: The summons, the refusal, the charge
entries.digest: Lee sent Lieutenant J. E. B. Stuart under a flag with a written summons promising the men safety to await the President's orders if they surrendered. It was refused. Marines broke in the engine-house doors and the fight was over in minutes; one Marine, Private Luke Quinn, was killed, and Brown was wounded and captured. Stuart recognised the prisoner as the Kansas fighter.
entries.quote: the whole was over in a few minutes
entries.source_note: Lee's demand for surrender, 18 Oct 1859 (National Archives RG 94, DocsTeach); Lee's report 19 Oct; Stuart's letter to his mother, Jan 1860 (Encyclopedia Virginia).

entries.headline: Watching the storm, then slipping away
entries.digest: From the arsenal Anderson saw the Marines batter in the engine-house doors. He and Hazlett got out at the back, crossed the Potomac that night in an old boat, and found the Kennedy farm ransacked. They headed north on foot, living on roasted corn.
entries.source_note: Anderson, A Voice from Harper's Ferry (1861); sequence from the book, dates of later stages not given.

entries.headline: Questioned on the floor for three hours
entries.digest: Lying wounded, Brown answered Senator Mason, Representative Vallandigham, Colonel Faulkner and others while reporters wrote. He refused to name backers, said he had come to free slaves, and invoked the Golden Rule. He warned Southerners to prepare for a settlement of the slavery question.
entries.quote: No man sent me here; it was my own prompting
entries.source_note: Interview as printed by the New York Herald and reprinted by Sanborn (1910); marxists.org transcription. WV Archives ch. 11 dates the questioning to 18 Oct.

entries.headline: The senator asks who paid
entries.digest: Mason's questions, as reporters recorded them, kept returning to money and accomplices: who furnished the arms, who sent him, how the raid was organised. Brown answered on his own motives and declined to name names. The same questions would drive Mason's Senate inquiry two months later.
entries.source_note: Herald interview (Sanborn 1910; marxists.org); WV Archives ch. 11.

entries.headline: The report to Washington
entries.digest: Lee reported to the Adjutant General: ten hostages freed; ten raiders killed, among them two of Brown's sons; five townsmen and a Marine dead; nine wounded. He listed the prisoners handed to the civil authorities and the pikes found at the farm. He judged the plan hopeless, its brief success due only to panic and exaggerated numbers.
entries.quote: the attempt of a fanatic or madman
entries.source_note: Lee to Col. S. Cooper, 19 Oct 1859 (Encyclopedia Virginia; printed in Senate Rep. 278, 1860).

entries.headline: Prisoners carried to the county jail
entries.digest: Brown, Aaron Stevens, Edwin Coppoc, Shields Green and John Copeland were taken from Harpers Ferry to the Jefferson County jail in Charles Town, to be tried by the state, not the federal government.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11.

entries.headline: The governor praises his prisoner
entries.digest: Back in Richmond, Wise told a crowd that Brown was a fanatic, vain and garrulous, but also brave, truthful and plain-spoken. He spoke with admiration of his calm under questioning, while blaming Northern agitators for the raid.
entries.source_note: Speech of Gov. Wise at Richmond, 21 Oct 1859, printed in the National Era, 3 Nov 1859 (Civil War Notebook extract).

entries.headline: Whose are the captured rifles?
entries.digest: Wise wrote to General Charles Egerton that arms taken from the raiders belonged to the accused until conviction, not to the troops who seized them. He also asked that rifles taken without authority from the federal arsenal by Maryland militia be returned.
entries.source_note: Wise to Egerton, 24 Oct 1859, Library of Virginia.

entries.headline: Arraigned before the examining court
entries.digest: Brown and the other prisoners were brought before the county court, with Brown still too weak to stand. Lawson Botts and Thomas C. Green were assigned to defend them.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11 (arraignment 25 Oct).

entries.headline: Indicted on three counts
entries.digest: The grand jury indicted the prisoners for treason against the Commonwealth of Virginia, for conspiring with slaves to rebel, and for the murders of Turner, Beckham, Boerly, Shepherd and Quinn. Brown's trial was set to begin the next day.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11.

entries.headline: Asking the governor's leave to nurse Brown
entries.digest: Child wrote to Governor Wise asking permission to go to Charles Town to nurse the wounded prisoner. She said plainly that she thought Brown's act mistaken but admired him, and enclosed a letter for Brown himself.
entries.source_note: Child to Wise, Wayland, 26 Oct 1859, in the 1860 pamphlet (WV Archives catalogue entry).

entries.headline: Trial opens with the prisoner on a cot
entries.digest: After a doctor pronounced him fit, Brown was carried in and lay on a cot. His counsel read a telegram from Ohio reporting insanity in his mother's family; Brown rose to reject any plea of insanity. The judge pressed on.
entries.source_note: Famous Trials chronology; WV Archives ch. 11 (insanity evidence rejected by Brown). Telegram detail from newspaper reports.

entries.headline: Permission granted, with a rebuke
entries.digest: Wise answered Child that she could go to Charles Town under the protection of Virginia's laws, but scolded her for sympathising with a man who had come to incite slaves to murder. He forwarded her letter to Brown.
entries.source_note: Wise to Child, Richmond, 29 Oct 1859, in the 1860 pamphlet (WV Archives catalogue entry).

entries.headline: 'A Plea for Captain John Brown'
entries.digest: With most of the press calling Brown mad, Thoreau read a long defence of him in Concord. He praised Brown as a man of principle and attacked the newspapers and the government. He repeated the lecture in Boston on 1 November and Worcester on 3 November.
entries.quote: I plead not for his life, but for his character
entries.source_note: Thoreau, 'A Plea for Captain John Brown', printed in Echoes of Harper's Ferry (1860); Famous Trials.

entries.headline: Guilty on every count
entries.digest: Samuel Chilton closed for the defence, arguing that Brown, not a Virginian, could not commit treason against Virginia and had killed no one himself. Andrew Hunter answered for the Commonwealth. The jury was out less than an hour and returned guilty on all three counts.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11 (verdict 31 Oct, under an hour). Famous Trials chronology puts the verdict on 2 Nov, contrary to the court dates; 31 Oct followed here.

entries.headline: A letter home on the day of the verdict
entries.digest: Brown wrote to his family about the raid and the conviction, and added a postscript on 2 November that he had been sentenced to hang. It is one of the first of his many jail letters to his wife and children at North Elba.
entries.source_note: Brown to his family, 31 Oct 1859, with 2 Nov postscript; Boyd B. Stutler Collection, WV Archives (gallery item jb29).

entries.headline: 'My wisdom or my cowardice'
entries.digest: Named in captured papers and sought by Virginia, Douglass wrote from Canada to the Rochester Democrat. He denied ever promising to join the raid, called such a promise rash and wild, and admitted that wisdom or cowardice had kept him away. He did not disown Brown.
entries.quote: there is no man living, and no man dead
entries.source_note: Douglass letter dated Canada West, 31 Oct 1859; reprinted New Orleans Picayune, 9 Nov 1859 (House Divided).

entries.headline: Copeland and Green: neither citizens nor traitors?
entries.digest: Shields Green, Copeland, Coppoc and John E. Cook were tried in November and convicted of inciting slaves and murder. George Sennott argued that under the Dred Scott decision Green and Copeland were not citizens and so could not be guilty of treason. All four were sentenced to hang on 16 December.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11 (Sennott's argument; Voorhees for Cook). Exact trial days not fixed here.

entries.headline: The speech before sentence
entries.digest: Asked if he had anything to say, Brown spoke without notes. He denied intending murder or insurrection, said that had he acted for the rich and powerful no one would blame him, and appealed to the Bible's command to remember those in bonds. Reporters' versions differ slightly in wording.
entries.source_note: Speech at sentencing, 2 Nov 1859, as reported in the press (Digital History; Famous Trials).

entries.headline: Sentenced to hang on 2 December
entries.digest: Judge Richard Parker sentenced Brown to be hanged in public on Friday 2 December. Defence counsel then petitioned the Virginia Court of Appeals for a writ of error, arguing again that Brown owed Virginia no allegiance; the petition failed.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11; Famous Trials chronology.

entries.headline: A reward for the raiders still at large
entries.digest: Wise proclaimed a reward for the arrest of Owen Brown, Barclay Coppoc, Francis Meriam and Charles Tidd, charged with treason, murder and conspiring with slaves. The heading of the printed proclamation and its text disagree on the sum.
entries.source_note: Proclamation dated 3 Nov 1859, Library of Virginia.

entries.headline: A Virginian answers Mrs. Child
entries.digest: Having read Child's letter in the papers, Mrs. Mason wrote to her directly and with fury. She called Child a hypocrite, described the care she said Virginia women gave their slaves, and wrote of what a servile war would have meant for Southern women and children.
entries.source_note: Mrs. M. J. C. Mason to Child, 11 Nov 1859, in the 1860 pamphlet, pp. 16–19 (Civil War Notebook).

entries.headline: Counting the dead, and the crops
entries.digest: Brown told his wife how their sons had died: Oliver near him soon after being shot, Watson on the 19th. He asked whether any crops had ripened, thanked donors for a trunk of clothes, and blamed rumours of arson round Charles Town on others. He told her not to come yet.
entries.source_note: Brown to Mary Ann Day Brown, 21 Nov 1859, Sanborn, Life and Letters (1885), pp. 595–6 (Civil War Notebook).

entries.headline: Ruffin sets out for Charles Town
entries.digest: Ruffin left his plantation to see the execution for himself. His diary treats the raid as proof that the North meant war on the South. He was determined to be present when Brown died.
entries.source_note: Ruffin, Diary, vol. 1 (Scarborough ed., 1972), as summarised in Civil War Monitor; departure date given by the article, diary page not cited.

entries.headline: Last letter to his wife and children
entries.digest: Brown wrote that he faced death with composure and believed it would serve God's cause. He told his family to read the Bible, to live content with little, to love one another, and to abhor slavery. He noted two sums of money arranged for his wife.
entries.source_note: Brown to his family, 30 Nov 1859 (Macmillan reader, from Sanborn).

entries.headline: A Senate inquiry into the raid
entries.digest: When the new Congress met, Mason moved for a select committee to inquire into the raid and whether citizens of other states had helped to arm it. The committee, with Mason as chair, Jefferson Davis and G. N. Fitch in the majority and Jacob Collamer and J. R. Doolittle in the minority, began calling witnesses.
entries.source_note: Senate Historical Office (committee created when the Senate convened, 5 Dec 1859); WV Archives Mason report (members). Exact day of adoption not fixed here.

entries.headline: Pikes as propaganda
entries.digest: Ruffin obtained fifteen of Brown's pikes from the Harpers Ferry arsenal and arranged through Senator Clement Clay to send one to the governor of every slaveholding state, each labelled as a sample of what the North intended. Months later he saw them on show in a Senate committee room.
entries.source_note: Ruffin, Diary, vol. 1, pp. 379–383, 431, summarised in Civil War Monitor; dates not given.

entries.headline: Mary Brown's visit
entries.digest: Mary Brown, who had travelled from North Elba, was allowed to see her husband on the afternoon before the execution and they ate a last meal together. She left before nightfall and was not permitted to stay.
entries.source_note: Famous Trials chronology (via mail.famous-trials.com); hours from general accounts, not checked against a primary source here.

entries.headline: The last note to a guard
entries.digest: On the morning of his execution Brown handed a guard a short written note. It said he was now certain that the crimes of this guilty land would be purged only with blood, and that he had vainly hoped it might be done without much bloodshed.
entries.quote: will never be purged away; but with Blood
entries.source_note: Manuscript note of 2 Dec 1859, printed by Sanborn (1885). Original spelling and punctuation kept.

entries.headline: Praying for the condemned man
entries.digest: Jackson wrote to his wife that afternoon. Brown rode to the field on his coffin, climbed the scaffold with apparent cheerfulness and stood hooded on the trap for about ten minutes while the troops took their places. Jackson wrote that he had prayed for Brown's salvation.
entries.quote: I sent up a petition that he might be saved
entries.source_note: Jackson to Mary Anna Jackson, 2 Dec [1859], Library of Virginia; printed 1892 (VMI Archives).

entries.headline: A secessionist in the cadets' ranks
entries.digest: After a night out with a VMI patrol, back in his room about 4 a.m., Ruffin stood with the cadets at the hanging. His diary records the scene and the soldiers, but, as his editors and historians note, offers no reflection on Brown's fate beyond it.
entries.source_note: Ruffin, Diary, vol. 1, pp. 360–370, summarised in Civil War Monitor.

entries.headline: An exile pleads, not knowing the date
entries.digest: Hugo addressed an open letter to the United States asking the republic to spare Brown, warning that his execution would wound the Union itself. He wrote it on the day Brown died, unaware that the sentence had been carried out that morning.
entries.source_note: Hugo's open letter to the London News, 2 Dec 1859 (Tufts exhibit; Wikisource English text). French original; no quotation.

entries.headline: A memorial service at the hour of death
entries.digest: Thoreau organised a service in Concord timed to the hanging, with readings, a dirge and no speeches. It was one of many such gatherings across the North that day.
entries.source_note: Thoreau's 'Martyrdom of John Brown' (printed 1860); details from general Concord accounts, not checked against the primary text here.

entries.headline: Burial at the Adirondack farm
entries.digest: Brown's body was taken north by his widow and buried by the boulder at the family farm at North Elba, near Lake Placid. Wendell Phillips spoke at the grave.
entries.source_note: Famous Trials chronology (burial at North Elba); day from general accounts.

entries.headline: Writing to his brother Henry
entries.digest: Copeland told his brother he was to die for helping to free slaves, as Washington's soldiers had fought for freedom. He wrote that Black soldiers had helped win independence and been betrayed, and asked Henry to repay any kindness shown him by his jailer, John Avis.
entries.quote: they were by the whites most treacherously deceived
entries.source_note: Copeland to Henry Copeland, Charlestown, 10 Dec 1859 (Oberlin College transcription).

entries.headline: 'I am well, both in body and in mind'
entries.digest: On the morning of his execution Copeland wrote to his parents, brothers and sisters. He said he was at peace and not afraid, blamed no one but himself and bore no ill will, condemned slavery as unjust, and asked them to meet him in heaven.
entries.quote: I have no antipathy against anyone
entries.source_note: Copeland to his family, Charlestown Jail, 16 Dec 1859 (Oberlin College transcription).

entries.headline: Four more executions
entries.digest: Shields Green and John Copeland were hanged in the morning, John Cook and Edwin Coppoc in the afternoon, as the court had ordered. Anderson, by then in safety, later called the trials of Green and Copeland a mockery.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11 (sentence for 16 Dec); Anderson (1861) on the executions.

entries.headline: Answering Mrs. Mason point by point
entries.digest: Child replied at length, setting the slave laws and fugitive-slave advertisements against Mrs. Mason's picture of benevolent mastery. She argued that the principle, not Brown himself, was the real question.
entries.quote: the principle for which John Brown died is the question at issue
entries.source_note: Child to Mason, Wayland, 17 Dec 1859, in the 1860 pamphlet (WV Archives; American Yawp excerpt).

entries.headline: Lee before the Mason committee
entries.digest: Lee gave evidence to the Senate committee on the events at Harpers Ferry, as did hostages and officers. His testimony was printed with the committee's report.
entries.source_note: Lee and Mason committee testimony, WV Archives (leemasontestimony page); exact day not seen.

entries.headline: The last two raiders hanged
entries.digest: Aaron Stevens, whose trial had been delayed while Wise considered a federal trial, and Albert Hazlett, caught in Pennsylvania and returned, were convicted of treason, murder and inciting slaves, and hanged on 16 March. Their executions closed the court's work on the raid.
entries.source_note: WV Archives ch. 11.

entries.headline: Two reports, two verdicts on the North
entries.digest: The majority called the raid the act of lawless ruffians backed by money and arms from outside Virginia, criticised the Massachusetts supporters, and said Congress had no power to legislate against it, recommending guards on federal arsenals. The minority (Collamer and Doolittle) found no evidence that the free states shared in it and said the inquiry had strayed into lawful antislavery opinion. Thaddeus Hyatt, jailed for refusing to testify, was freed when the Senate adjourned ten days later.
entries.source_note: Senate Rep. Com. No. 278, 36th Cong., 1st sess., 15 June 1860 (WV Archives transcription); Senate Historical Office on Hyatt's release, 25 June 1860.

entries.headline: A raider's account in print
entries.digest: Anderson published A Voice from Harper's Ferry, setting the raid out from inside and naming the Black raiders and the local men who, he said, took up pikes. He defended Brown and denounced the trials. He later served in the Union army.
entries.source_note: A Voice from Harper's Ferry (Boston, 1861), Gutenberg 73843; month of publication not fixed.

convergences.label: The engine house is stormed and Brown questioned
convergences.note: Lee writes it as a military operation finished in minutes; Brown, bleeding on the floor, turns the same afternoon's interrogation into a statement of purpose; Mason looks for paymasters; Anderson watches from the arsenal and runs.

convergences.label: Indictment in Charles Town, a letter from Wayland
convergences.note: On the day the grand jury charged treason, Child asked to come and nurse the accused, beginning a correspondence that would argue the case before the public rather than the jury.

convergences.label: Verdict day
convergences.note: The jury convicts in under an hour; Brown writes home; Douglass, named in the captured papers, writes from Canada to say he never promised to come; Thoreau's plea of the day before is being repeated in Boston.

convergences.label: Sentence and speech
convergences.note: The court fixes 2 December; Brown answers with the speech that Northern papers printed in full; the next day Wise offers rewards for the raiders still free.

convergences.label: The execution
convergences.note: Brown's note predicts blood; Jackson prays for his soul; Ruffin stands in the ranks and says little; Thoreau's Concord holds a memorial; Hugo in Guernsey pleads for a life already ended.

convergences.label: Copeland, Green, Cook and Coppoc hanged
convergences.note: Copeland's last letter, the court's sentence carried out, Anderson's later judgment of the trials; the next day Child's reply to Mrs. Mason argues that the principle, not the man, is on trial.

convergences.label: The Senate reports
convergences.note: Mason's majority and the Republican minority read the same testimony, Lee's among it, and reach opposite conclusions about Northern complicity.

ties.note: Mason questioned the wounded Brown on 18 October; the senator's later inquiry pursued the questions Brown had refused to answer.
Lee's summons and Marines ended the raid; his report called the plan the work of a fanatic or madman.
Wise questioned Brown at Harpers Ferry and then publicly praised his courage while refusing clemency.
Child asked Wise's leave to nurse Brown; his reply granted it with a rebuke, and both letters were printed.
Mrs. Mason wrote unasked after reading Child's letter; Child's December reply completed the 1860 pamphlet.
Margaretta Mason was the senator's wife; she wrote to Child while he prepared his Senate inquiry.
Brown answered Child's letter from jail, declining her visit and asking her to help his family instead.
Douglass met Brown at a quarry near Chambersburg in August 1859 and declined to join; Shields Green, who was with Douglass, went with Brown.
Fellow Black raiders; Anderson escaped and in 1861 wrote of Copeland's capture and execution.
Brown spoke in Concord in 1857 and 1859 and met Thoreau there; Thoreau's plea draws on those meetings.
Both stood with the VMI cadet detachment at the scaffold on 2 December.
Lee testified before Mason's select committee; his report was printed with its findings.
Hugo's open letter and later drawing made Brown known across Europe; they never met.

claims.evidence: Interview as printed in the New York Herald; Sanborn (1910)

claims.claim: The plan was the attempt of a fanatic or madman that could only fail.
claims.evidence: Lee to Adjutant General Cooper, 19 Oct 1859

claims.claim: Brown is a fanatic, but brave, truthful, 'cool, collected, and indomitable'.
claims.evidence: Richmond speech, printed in the National Era, 3 Nov 1859

claims.evidence: Rochester Democrat; reprinted New Orleans Picayune, 9 Nov 1859

The crimes of this guilty land will be purged only with blood.

threads_out.note: Lee, Jackson and Stuart, all at Harpers Ferry or Charles Town in 1859, became Confederate commanders; Ruffin, who stood at the scaffold, later claimed one of the first shots at Fort Sumter. Union soldiers marched to 'John Brown's Body'.
Frederick Douglass, who declined Brown's invitation in August 1859 and fled to Canada after the raid, had been one of the signers at the Seneca Falls convention in 1848.

Brown's 'Provisional Constitution', adopted at Chatham, Canada West, in 1858 and found at the Kennedy farm, was modelled on the 1787 Constitution; his defence turned on what treason and allegiance meant under state and federal law.

The raiders cut the telegraph wires at Harpers Ferry; once the line was restored, the telegraph carried the news, the interview and the trial reports to every Northern and Southern paper within hours.
